newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia Metals -- China seen waiting to buy copper.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals -- China seen waiting to buy copper.

text.p: China, whose copper strategy has puzzled global traders, is likely to purchase more of the red metal later this year as the country's consumption looks set to rise higher than previously expected, traders said on Thursday.
"China is not a buyer at the current price level," said one trader. "But it's likely to buy the metal once the price gets lower or if this level is maintained for a while."
Despite rumours that China might unload its strategic copper reserves to cash in on currently strong world prices, traders in Tokyo said this did not appear to be happening.
On the contrary, they said, China is consistently picking up copper to meet steadily growing demand, although its appetite is not as voracious as it was in March and April.
The Japanese spot copper market, on the other hand, remained quiet, with premiums unchanged at $60 to $70 per tonne over London Metal Exchange (LME) prices.
"Japanese demand does not feel strong," said one trader. "The summer is also forecast to be cool, which should dampen demand for air conditioners."
Traders were unconcerned about news that the Ok Tedi mine in Papua New Guinea was delaying June copper concentrate deliveries to Japan because of dry river conditions.
"It might have a psychological impact if more such news on water or power shortages is added in, but I can't imagine this itself would lead to problems here," one copper trader said.
In the physical zinc market, although stocks are relatively low, premiums eased slightly to $40 to $90 per tonne amid plentiful offers from China, traders said.

"There's a fair amount of offers from China, but nobody is interested," said one trader at a European trading house. "If the economy recovers after the summer, the premiums might rise again as stocks are low, but we've seen no signs of that yet."

Traders said domestic steel production was set for a drop of four percent in the July-September quarter from the previous quarter, after a surge early this year triggered by brisk business in the automobile industry both domestically and abroad.

Asked about a report that North Korea sold to Seoul a large consignment of zinc originally promised to U.S. grain trader Cargill Inc in a barter deal, one trader with close ties to Pyongyang said: "They must have chosen to sell it to South Korea because they can get hold of hard currency much more quickly that way."

He estimated that North Korea's unofficial zinc exports to South Korea were at least as large as its sales to Japan. Pyongyang usually sets its official zinc export price at a discount of $20 to $30 per tonne to LME prices.
The physical aluminium market remained tight, with some offers seen at premiums as high as $110 per tonne.

"People are unwilling to sell as it's still unclear what's going to happen in the third quarter," said one trader at a major Japanese trading house. "The premiums might stay at these high levels until the summer."
The trader said aluminium stocks in Yokohama declined further towards 150,000 tonnes at the end of May, well under usual levels above 200,000 tonnes.
